title: Introduction to MaxMin
text: González (1985) algorithm builds selection greedily: start seed point, repeatedly add whichever unselected point farthest current selection. greedy rule guarantees 2-approximation optimal Tk runs O(N · m) time. default FarFirst() runs three "random_furthest" starts, beginning point furthest randomly selected ‘pivot’ point, returns whichever pass produced highest Tk. random starts can requested via nseeds argument. Peripheral seeds may also selected deterministic strategies: one strategies can selected via strategy argument. best solution found returned. pairwise distances objects known — coordinates work — computing storing N×N distances expensive, function may passed place distance matrix. function passed one index , returns distances object N objects — one column matrix. FarFirst() calls kk times, full N×N matrix never built. N, number objects, must supplied.

title: Introduction to MaxMin
text: see methods relate visually, generate 50 points two dimensions select k = 8 . Even small difference Tk can correspond meaningfully dispersed selection. Plotting selections point cloud makes differences concrete. two methods select index, symbols overlap; Tk table captures quality distinction even visual overlap high.  Selections returned method 50 random 2-D points (k = 8). Coloured symbols mark selected points; grey circles full candidate set. small jitter separates symbols shared indices.
code: set.seed(42) pts <- matrix(rnorm(100), ncol = 2)   # 50 points, 2 dimensions d50 <- dist(pts) k   <- 8L ffPick <- FarFirst(k, d50) da50Pick <- DropAdd(k, d50, plateau = 500L) set.seed(42) gr50Pick <- Grasp(k, d50, plateau = 50L) scores <- c(   FarFirst  = MinDist(d50, ffPick),   DropAdd = attr(da50Pick, "score"),   Grasp   = attr(gr50Pick, "score") ) round(scores, 3) #> FarFirst  DropAdd    Grasp  #>    1.416    1.428    1.428 methods <- list(   FarFirst  = ffPick,   DropAdd = da50Pick,   Grasp   = gr50Pick ) cols <- c(FarFirst = "#E41A1C", DropAdd = "#377EB8", Grasp = "#4DAF4A") pchs <- c(FarFirst = 24L, DropAdd = 21L, Grasp = 22L) # Small per-method shift so coincident selections remain distinguishable dx   <- c(FarFirst = 0, DropAdd =  0.04, Grasp = -0.04) dy   <- c(FarFirst = 0, DropAdd = -0.04, Grasp =  0.04)  plot(pts, pch = 1L, col = "grey75", asp = 1L,      xlab = "x", ylab = "y",      main = "MaxMin method comparison")  for (nm in names(methods)) {   sel <- methods[[nm]]   points(     pts[sel, 1L] + dx[nm],     pts[sel, 2L] + dy[nm],     pch = pchs[nm], col = cols[nm], bg = cols[nm], cex = 1.6   ) }  legend("topright",        legend = paste0(names(methods), "  (Tₖ = ", round(scores, 3), ")"),        pch = pchs, col = cols, pt.bg = cols, pt.cex = 1.4, bty = "n")

text: small instances (roughly N ≤ 25–30), ExactMaxMin() solves problem proven optimality via node-packing integer programme (Sayyady & Fathi, 2016), using highs solver. First must install highs: $proven = TRUE certifies selection can achieve higher Tk. ExactMaxMin() NP-hard; instances ~30 candidates require time budget tackled heuristics .

title: Introduction to MaxMin
text: Every method pursues dispersion — spreads selection members mutually far apart. k-centre problem instead pursues coverage: minimises covering radius R, largest distance point nearest chosen centre, point pool left far representative (González, 1985; Hochbaum & Shmoys, 1985). dispersion reaches extremes, covering reaches interior, data two optima generally different selections. KCentre() chooses centres deterministic CDSh heuristic (García-Díaz et al., 2017; García-Díaz et al., 2019), typically lands within 1–3.5 % optimum — order magnitude tighter Gonzalez 2-approximation FarFirst() gives objective. KCentreRadius() scores centre set covering radius (lower better). CDSh covers least tightly Gonzalez 2-approximation baseline: Like MinDist(), KCentreRadius() also accepts points coordinate matrix, case never materialises full N × N matrix — can score selection well past size solvers’ distance matrix fit memory. small instances, ExactKCentre() solves covering problem proven optimality sequence minimum-set-cover integer programs — covering dual ExactMaxMin()’s node-packing programme — warm-started KCentre() radius bisected smallest feasible radius. Like ExactMaxMin(), uses highs solver. covering optimum sometimes attained fewer centres (every point covered, extra centres lower radius); indices length requested number, reported radius still proven optimum. ExactKCentre() NP-hard, — like ExactMaxMin() — ground-truth reference small instances, scalable method. dispersion covering optima differ even small example: dispersion selects cities rim map, covering pulls inward keep every city near centre.
code: centres <- KCentre(4L, eurodist) labels(eurodist)[centres] #> [1] "Cologne"    "Copenhagen" "Madrid"     "Rome" centres #> 4 centres (6 7 14 19) by CDSh, covering radius <= 1011 ff <- FarFirst(4L, eurodist, strategy = "peripheral") c(KCentre  = KCentreRadius(eurodist, centres),   FarFirst = KCentreRadius(eurodist, ff)) #>  KCentre FarFirst  #>     1011     1209 kc <- ExactKCentre(4L, eurodist) kc #> 4 centres (6 7 14 19) by exact MILP (highs), proven optimal, covering radius = 1011 attr(kc, "proven")      # TRUE  ⟹  radius is the global covering optimum #> [1] TRUE disp <- sort(ExactMaxMin(4L, eurodist)$indices) labels(eurodist)[disp]              # dispersion: pushed to the extremes #> [1] "Athens"    "Lisbon"    "Milan"     "Stockholm" labels(eurodist)[sort(as.integer(kc))]  # covering: pulled toward the interior #> [1] "Cologne"    "Copenhagen" "Madrid"     "Rome"

text: solver results now print legibly. FarFirst(), DropAdd() Grasp() return "MaxMinSelection" object ExactMaxMin() "MaxMinExact" object, print()/format() method giving one-line summary (size, selected indices, algorithm – FarFirst() ensemble – winning strategy, plus achieved T_k). summary() method adds multi-line report: per-strategy T_k table FarFirst() ensemble, secondary objective search effort DropAdd()/Grasp(), instance, objective proof status ExactMaxMin(). objects otherwise unchanged: MaxMinSelection still integer index vector (indexes matrix coordinate set directly), MaxMinExact still list $indices, $objective, …. FarFirst() gains nseeds argument: distinct-seed random restart draws random pivots, collects one’s furthest-point seed de-duplicated nseeds distinct seeds found (reachable pool exhausted), runs Gonzalez returns best T_k. “give count, list” counterpart pivots – never wasting Gonzalez pass duplicate seed – overrides method/pivots supplied. Reproducible set.seed(); unsupported distance-column oracle path. ExactMaxMin() substantially faster scales larger instances. DropAdd() now documents maxSeconds checked every 256 iterations may overshoot one iteration’s worth computation large instances. FarFirst() documents asymmetric distance matrices accepted. Ensemble functions now attach score = NA_real_ attribute trivial -points early return (m >= N). Integer iteration counters C++ kernels changed int long long avoid signed-integer overflow upper bound extreme maxIter values. Test suite: improved coverage path relinking (strict improvement), DropAdd secondary attribute formula, ExactMaxMin budget-expiry branch, various weak / vacuous assertions tightened.

title: MaxMin 0.0.0.9001 (development)
text: Grasp() longer crashes documented alpha = 1 (pure greedy). Grasp() now validates alpha, rejecting values outside [0, 1]. FarFirst(), DropAdd(), Grasp() MinDist() now reject distance matrix containing NA/NaN/Inf instead silently returning selection repeated index; distance-column oracle path FarFirst() likewise rejects non-self NA/NaN. MinDist() now errors NA duplicate indices idx (previously matrix-path NA returned NA silently duplicates scored 0). Added defensive guards exported C++ kernels reachable via ::: (MaximinFrom_cpp, MaximinFromPoints_cpp, DropAdd_points_cpp).

title: MaxMin 0.0.0.9001 (development)
text: FarFirst(): subset-size argument renamed n -> m, matching solvers; seed argument renamed method (matching PickPoint(method =)), since selects seeding strategy, RNG seed. DropAdd() Grasp(): seed argument removed. DropAdd()’s documented -op (search RNG-free); reproducible Grasp() run, call set.seed() Grasp(). FarFirst() now attaches achieved objective (T_k) score attribute bare ensemble returns, matching DropAdd() Grasp() (previously value discarded bare pass). Index-order conventions now documented: FarFirst() returns farthest-first (greedy) order; DropAdd(), Grasp() ExactMaxMin()$indices return ascending indices. ExactMaxMin() continues return list (deliberate exception), now documented .

title: MaxMin 0.0.0.9000 (development)
text: Initial release: tiered toolbox Max-Min Diversity Problem (MMDP / discrete p-dispersion), extracted FurthestPoint study package can depended CRAN packages (e.g. TreeSearch). FarFirst(): deterministic farthest-first selection distance matrix, Euclidean coordinates (points =), -demand distance-column oracle (pass column function d, N =) spaces coordinate embedding; oracle may report self-distance (length N) omit (length N - 1), whichever simpler compute. default seed runs best--three ensemble "random_furthest" starts (whose pivots drawn session RNG; set seed reproducible selection, supply via pivots argument) keeps best MinDist(). deterministic O(N) anchors ("anti_centroid", "peripheral") costlier O(N²) anchors ("diameter", "anti_medoid", "medoid", "rowsum", "rownorm") available opt-strategies. DropAdd(): DropAdd tabu search (Porumbel et al. 2011); accepts dist object, distance matrix, coordinate matrix (points =). ExactMaxMin(): exact node-packing optimum (Sayyady & Fathi 2016) via highs MILP backend. Grasp(): GRASP path relinking (Resende et al. 2010), dense-matrix-refinement metaheuristic attains highest T_k package’s methods small medium instances. MinDist(): k-centre objective (minimum pairwise distance). PickPoint(): exposes peripheral seed indices directly.
